summary:
Argentina's Law 26.743 remains one of the most permissive legal gender recognition regimes in the world. It was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, and promulgated on 24 May 2012. It allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval, and the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Identity documents have carried an 'X' gender marker since 2021.

Río Negro stands under that national framework and adds one of only a handful of provincial statutes reserving at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people.

The national framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal of the statute. On 5 February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued decree DNU 62/2025 restricting minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned the courts to intervene. The outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán, who was stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins, told the Washington Blade in reporting dated 10 April 2025 that the community faces a chaotic and desperate situation. They reported that the national government eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry, dismissed trans public servants hired under the federal Trans Labour Quota Law, which reserves 1% of public-sector posts, and is no longer implementing that quota. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force, they said, but is no longer guaranteed in practice.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a rise of 62% year-on-year and the worst figure in the observatory's ten years, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026.

Trans women and travestis were 142 of the 227 victims, or 62.5%. Physical violence against bodily integrity accounted for 147 cases, or 64.8%, with beatings the main modality. Perpetrators were predominantly security-force personnel and unidentified attackers in public space, and Agencia Presentes attributes the surge to the government's 'cultural battle' and hate discourse. The same period saw DNU 62/2025 restricting minors' gender-affirming treatments.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance, which an appeal court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is not applied in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through a combination of national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

The hate-crime figures for 2025 are drawn from a single national observatory with a ten-year record, and Agencia Presentes published them on 19 March 2026 as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. The attribution of the increase to government discourse is the assessment of that agency rather than a judicial finding.

Activists' statements about non-implementation of the federal quota and about the Gender Identity Law being no longer guaranteed are testimony reported by the Washington Blade; they are consistent with the elimination of the responsible ministry and the dismissals they describe, but no official instrument repealing Law 26.743 is recorded in the sources available here.
localsOnly:
Residents of Río Negro obtain identity documents under the national framework, which has offered an 'X' gender marker on the DNI since 2021 and permits change of registered gender without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order.

Río Negro's provincial statute reserves at least 1% of public-administration posts for travesti, transsexual and transgender people. Whether those posts are being filled under the present provincial administration is not established in the sources available here.

Employment support at national level has been withdrawn: the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry was eliminated, trans public servants hired under the federal Trans Labour Quota Law were dismissed, and activists report that the 1% federal quota is no longer being implemented.

Adult residents retain statutory access to gender-affirming care under Law 26.743 as it stands. For minors, access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment is restricted by the decree of 5 February 2025.

For residents in detention, the decree of February 2025 governing the housing of transgender people in prison applies, although its specific provisions are not detailed in the sources available here.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation brought against the decree of 5 February 2025 on gender-affirming care for minors is unresolved in the sources available here; the courts' response to the petitions described is not recorded.

Implementation of Río Negro's 1% provincial quota is unresolved. The sources reviewed establish that the statute exists but do not document posts filled, refusal of posts, or enforcement proceedings.

Whether the federal Trans Labour Quota Law has been formally repealed or is merely not being implemented is unresolved. The sources record dismissals and activists' reports of non-implementation, not a repealing instrument.

The precise scope of DNU 62/2025, including which procedures and which ages it covers, is not detailed in the inventory, and neither are the provisions of the separate decree on the prison housing of transgender people.

Requirements affecting the registration of trans-led organisations in Río Negro, which the Outright International overview flags at national level as of 12 March 2026, are not sourced for the province.

Statistics on hate crimes are national; no province-level breakdown for Río Negro appears in the sources available here.
